nice and simple challenge, the only hurdle I had was during test case 15 "Half a deck left", the final calculation for true count had me dividing by 0 which caused an error, wasn't a problem though I just made the true count equal the running count if the calculation was ever dividing by 0 and got it correct

It's a simple challenge suitable for CoC. I do agree with @YourGirlJames that the description can be quite a challenge to read and understand in a short amount of time. Some basic suggestions from me:

- The background of Blackjack and the Hi-Low card counting system can be shortened / removed. One suggestion is to begin your problem description straightaway with: "The <<Hi-Low>> card counting system in Blackjack assigns different values to each of the card ranks:"

- The description of how to compute the true count can also be shortened. For example, removing non-necessary keywords such as "shoe" can make it easier for players unfamiliar with terms to comprehend the problem.

One sample problem description:

The <<Hi-Low>> card counting system in <<Blackjack>> assigns different values to each of the card ranks:
- {{2}}, {{3}}, {{4}}, {{5}} and {{6}} are assigned a value of {{+1}}.
- {{7}}, {{8}} and {{9}} are assigned a value of {{0}}.
- {{T}}, {{J}}, {{Q}}, {{K}} and {{A}} are assigned a value of {{-1}}.

A game of Blackjack uses {{6}} decks of {{52}} cards each. To use the Hi-Low card counting system, a <<running count>> (starting from {{0}}) keeps track of the <<total value>> of all card(s) that have been dealt. Players must keep track of the running count to compute the <<true count>>:
- Compute the number of <<decks remaining>> by dividing the number of cards remaining by {{52}} and rounding to the nearest integer. If the rounded number is {{0}}, assume the number of decks is {{1}} instead.
- Compute the <<true count>> by dividing the <<running count>> by the number of <<decks remaining>> and rounding to the nearest integer.

The <<true count>> is then used to determine the winning chances of a player's hand.

---

Alternatively, a simple way to fix this problem: disable Fastest mode. Then there is no rush to read and understand the problem description :)

✅ Approved the contribution.
Comment: I accept this contribution because it provides a clear, well‑structured explanation of the Hi‑Low counting system, including accurate value assignments for each card rank .
The step‑by‑step description of the running count and true count calculations is precise and easy to follow, especially the detailed worked example showing how the remaining decks and final true count are computed
The input/output format is unambiguous, and the test suite is extensive, covering short, medium, long, and edge‑case scenarios such as low‑card‑dominated decks, high‑card‑dominated decks, and even cases with only one card left in the shoe .
Overall, the contribution is coherent, pedagogical, and polished — a strong and engaging Clash of Code challenge.
I hope you received enough feedback from the community to improve your contribution. Once you have made the necessary updates, publish your contribution!

Honestly, great contribution!
The statement is clear, well‑structured, and pleasant to read, and you manage to make a technical topic (Hi‑Low counting) accessible even to people who aren’t familiar with blackjack. The examples are well chosen and make the logic immediately understandable.
Kudos as well for the precision of your explanations and the consistency between the description and the tests.
Excellent work — keep it up!

Goal

* Please clarify the tie-breaking behavior for "round to the nearest integer". Specifically, how should values like 0.5 or 1.5 be handled? In the "Short" case, a value of 0.5 is rounded to 0, which suggests a specific rule is being applied.

Cases

* Replacing 312 with 311 in the author's solution doesn't trigger any test failures. To catch this bug, consider adding a test/validator pair with a sequence of 234 cards of value 1.

Thank you.

Very interesting challenge that would be super fun to code!  I am just concerned that the true count part may be too complex to understand in the time limit if you dont already have a basic understanding of card counting. I appreciate that there is an explanation provided which is helpful but the explanation is very long so it may take too long to understand it and still code the solution.

Goal
* Consider formatting 6 (in "6 decks") and 52 as a {{constants}}. Especially 6 because that's different from most card game contributions which assume using a single deck.

* For clarity, consider converting the value assignment explanation to a three-bullet point list, one bullet point for each value, or to a monospace-format table.

* "add up the numbers": Consider changing "numbers" to "values" for consistency and clarity.

* Example
  • Consider changing 10 to T for clarity.

  • 7-9 appeared 17 times, not 6 times (and make corresponding adjustments to the rest of the example too; 27 + 6 + 36 ≠ 79 in the first place anyway 🤭).

Input
* Please change 10 to T.

Constraints
* Please add the lower and upper bounds for the length of [[cards]] as a constraint. (The upper bound should be less than 52 * 6.)

Thanks.
All suggestions have been implemented. Thank you for your feedback as always! 😊

Thank you for your feedback. 

I appreciate your comment on the "true count" part of the problem. The reason I include the true count in the problem is to make the problem a little bit harder. 

If you have any suggestions for making my explanation less wordy, that would be great! 

Thank you!
All test cases with decimal value of 0.5 have been changed to a different value. Thank you for your comment.

Also, would it be possible to include the total number of dealt cards in your input? E.g.:

5
JJ775

This will help players who code in languages that do not support automatic parsing of inputs.
Please remove "length of" in the Constraints section. Thanks.
